Vignette: Mae

Mae is a seventy-one-year-old woman of Thai descent who spent the majority of her adult life building a meticulous career as a financial analyst. She is precise by nature, someone who has always found comfort in numbers, in the predictability of columns that balance and equations that resolve. That sense of order was shattered thirty-two years ago, and she has never quite recovered it.

In 1992, while traveling through a neighboring country for a regional banking conference, Mae was detained by armed militia members at a rural checkpoint. What began as a routine document inspection escalated without warning. She and two colleagues were held for nineteen days in a concrete outbuilding with no windows, given minimal food and water, and subjected to repeated interrogations that included threats of execution. One of her colleagues was beaten badly enough to require hospitalization after their release. Mae was not physically assaulted, but she witnessed the violence and lived for nearly three weeks not knowing whether she would survive. When she was finally released through diplomatic intervention, she was told simply to go home and say nothing.

And so she did. She went home. She said nothing. She returned to work within two weeks because, as she explains it, stopping felt more dangerous than continuing. For years, she poured herself into her analyses, her spreadsheets, her quarterly reports. Work was the one place where she could still feel capable. She married, had two children, and divorced in her early fifties - her ex-husband describing her, she says without much emotion, as "unreachable."

Now retired and living alone in a tidy apartment, Mae finds that the structure she once used to contain herself has largely dissolved. Without the discipline of a work schedule, the memories have more room to move. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart pounding, convinced for several disorienting seconds that she is back in that room. She can smell the damp concrete. She can hear the sound of boots on gravel outside the door. She lies rigid in her bed, waiting for a threat that does not come, unable to return to sleep.

During the day, she avoids the news, particularly any coverage involving political detention or conflict in Southeast Asia. She has declined two invitations to her granddaughter's school events held in the gymnasium - the low ceilings and echoing sounds feel unbearable to her, though she cannot always explain why to her family. She has become hypervigilant in ways she recognizes as disproportionate: checking the locks on her door three and four times before bed, sitting only with her back to the wall in restaurants, scanning exits whenever she enters a new space.

What troubles her most, she says quietly, is the numbness. She loves her grandchildren, she believes, but when she is with them she often feels as though she is watching the scene from a slight distance, present in body but not quite in feeling. She describes her emotional life as "flattened," and she mourns this more than the nightmares. The nightmares, at least, remind her that something happened. The numbness makes her wonder whether she is still fully a person.

She has never spoken about the captivity in any sustained way - not to her children, not to her former husband, not to a doctor. She mentions it now, in the therapist's office, with the careful precision of someone reading a financial report: facts delivered in order, affect held at arm's length. Only when she describes the sound of her colleague crying in the dark does her voice briefly lose its steadiness. She recovers quickly, straightens in her chair, and apologizes for the digression.

She is not sure why she finally came. She says she has started to feel, at seventy-one, that she is running out of time to feel something real again.
